transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-24
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (SapphireCloud Head Partnerships), Elena Garcia (Sapphire Solutions Architect), Tom Williams (Sapphire Product Partnerships)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, happy holidays — thanks for making time. quick intros: I'm Maya, I run partnerships at Redwood, this is Liam, he's our solutions engineer.
00:12 Rajiv: Thanks Maya, appreciate it. i'm Rajiv, head of cloud partnerships at SapphireCloud, and then Elena and Tom here. quick note we just spun up a partner enablement track so this is timed well.
00:25 Liam: great, i'll kick off with a short overview of how Redwood usually integrates with partners — we support hosted api, dedicated/reserved capacity, and private VPC installs. we'll try to focus on which model fits your go-to-market and compliance needs.
00:40 Elena: high level, Sapphire is looking to offer managed GPU instances plus a marketplace. key asks: tenant isolation, KMS integration, SOC2 compliance, and the ability to onboard enterprise customers with VPC peering or private link.
00:56 Maya: perfect, that's a common pattern. curious about scale — what's your typical customer size and GPU footprint?
01:08 Rajiv: our early anchor customers are mid-market to enterprise — average deployments start around 4 A100-equivalent GPUs and scale up to 40+ for larger models. latency matters for real-time inference use-cases. cost is also a huge seller for customers.
01:28 Liam: got it. when you say A100-equivalent, are you running multi-tenant on the same instances or offering dedicated nodes per tenant?
01:37 Tom: we do both today; our managed offering often starts multi-tenant and we offer dedicated for higher tiers. for Redwood integration it'd be ideal if we could offer both modes: quick hosted access for SMB and dedicated for enterprise.
01:50 Liam: that maps well to Redwood's Dedicated and Private modes — Dedicated is reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput; Private gives you our control plane but the runtime inside your VPC, or fully on-prem. we'd want to discuss how billing/quoting works for a resale or marketplace listing.
02:10 Elena: security — we need KMS/HSM for customer keys, audit logs per tenant, RBAC, SSO for our internal ops. also data residency for EU customers.
02:24 Maya: yes, SOC2 and KMS are supported; we integrate with common KMS providers and have audit logs and token-scoped tracing in the console. quick caveat: some of the naming in the docs, the auto-transcripts sometimes call KMS "K S M" — sorry for the transcriber — but the functionality is solid.
02:40 Rajiv: haha noted. can you speak to performance — we care about latency SLOs for 8k context models.
02:48 Liam: short answer: depends on model and kernel selection. our runtime picks optimized kernels, supports quantized execution and KV caching; for 8k-ish workloads we typically see Xms p50 on A100-class hardware for some open models, but we'll need to run benchmarks with your workload. we'd propose a short perf bench: sample prompts, typical batch sizes, and target latencies.
03:10 Tom: how invasive is the private deployment? our infra team prefers minimal agent installs; they want a package that can be deployed via terraform/helm.
03:20 Liam: we have a helm chart for the on-prem/private runtime and terraform modules for infra. customers often run the runtime in a VPC with a private control plane talking back to Redwood (optionally hosted control plane) — or completely air-gapped with an enterprise license.
03:36 Elena: any gotchas on network: NAT, egress, or KV cache requirements?
03:42 Liam: network-wise, for private you need an outbound to the control plane unless air-gapped; for VPC peering we use private link-style connections and support explicit egress rules. KV cache is local to the runtime nodes, nothing special network-wise. also mention of prefix caching and continuous batching which reduce per-token cost.
04:05 Rajiv: okay. commercial question: if we list Redwood in our marketplace, do we do resale (we bill customers and manage the infra) or do you prefer a referral model?
04:16 Maya: both are possible. common path: start with referral/partner integration (docs + demo) then move to a co-managed/resale agreement for enterprise customers. pricing and revenue share depend on committed capacity and who handles support.
04:30 Tom: support — who handles L2 for SRE? we need a clear division in the SLA.
04:36 Maya: we'd typically do 24/7 infra SLAs as part of Dedicated/resale, with an option to have your SRE own first line and Redwood own kernel/runtime level support. we can draft a support matrix.
04:50 Elena: on compliance — do you have SOC2 cert and region isolation?
04:55 Liam: yes SOC2; region isolation is supported via deployment zones and tenancy configs. we'll share our security whitepaper.
05:05 Rajiv: sounds good. let's talk integration effort — how long to get a proof-of-concept up and running for a single enterprise customer?
05:13 Liam: assuming we have infra access and the model artifacts, we can spin a POC in 2-4 weeks: infra + config + basic benchmark. if you want private control plane or air-gapped, add 1-2 weeks for networking and security reviews.
05:29 Maya: for the partner GTM we'd want to define co-marketing, enablement materials, a partner playbook, and a pilot success metric (uptime, latency p95, cost per token bucket).
05:43 Tom: what metrics do you typically track for pilots?
05:48 Liam: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec throughput, cost per generated token, error rates, and cold start times. we also track quality regressions via eval prompts.
05:58 Rajiv: any reference customers in EMEA? we need EU proof points for some prospects.
06:05 Maya: we'll share references; a couple partners in EU that are using our Dedicated offering.
06:12 Elena: ok, let's cover technical integration patterns quickly — API forwarding vs model routing vs on-prem runtime embedding.
06:20 Liam: three typical patterns: 1) API forwarding — you route calls from your marketplace to Redwood hosted endpoints (fastest to market). 2) Resale/Dedicated — deploy Redwood runtime in your infra and bill through you, gives tenant isolation and predictable throughput. 3) Private/On-prem — fully managed runtime inside customer or your private cloud for regulated workloads. each has trade-offs on latency, cost, and control.
06:46 Rajiv: for our marketplace MVP we likely want API forwarding and a dedicated offering for enterprise. can we do a hybrid listing?
06:54 Maya: yes, hybrid is common. we can support a listing that advertises both hosted self-serve and enterprise dedicated options.
07:02 Tom: how about metering and billing integration — do you expose usage APIs?
07:08 Liam: yes, we expose usage logs and a billing API; we can also push detailed token-level reports to a partner endpoint or S3.
07:18 Elena: one more on security — customer-managed keys per tenant?
07:22 Liam: we support tenant-scoped encryption keys with KMS integrations or customer-provided HSM in private deployments.
07:28 Rajiv: great. any immediate blockers from a legal/compliance standpoint?
07:32 Maya: none obvious; we'll need an NDA addendum to enable co-marketing and a resale clause if you plan to bill customers. legal teams should sync.
07:40 Tom: can you send a short integration checklist so our infra team knows the steps?
07:44 Maya: yes — we'll send the partner playbook which includes an integration checklist, roles/responsibilities, and a sample SOW template.
07:50 Rajiv: perfect. let's talk bench specifics so Liam can prepare what we need.
07:55 Liam: please share: representative model artifacts (or model names), expected concurrency, typical prompt sizes (context length), target latency SLOs, and sample dataset for quality evals. we'll run a small perf harness on an A100 and a 4-bit quantized run to give you ballpark numbers.
08:17 Elena: I'll collate and share by Monday; for models, we have a mix of Llama-3 70B fine-tuned and some open LLMs for embeddings and generation. concurrency is usually 8-16 concurrent sessions for mid-market, but spikes up during demo.
08:34 Liam: good — that will help us size the Dedicated pool. also note that quantization can change performance/latency tradeoffs.
08:42 Rajiv: any red flags on licensing for models? some customers require model licensing transparency.
08:47 Maya: we include model provenance in the catalog; for partner deployments we can mark model sources and license metadata in the console.
08:55 Tom: ok. about the demo — can you show a quick end-to-end flow next week?
08:59 Maya: yes, we'll do a short demo for the PM and infra teams and then the SE deep dive. propose a 45-minute demo + 60-minute technical deep dive for the week of Jan 11.
09:12 Rajiv: works. one more: marketplace listing process — what's required on our side?
09:17 Maya: typically: listing meta (description, features), pricing tier mapping, support SLAs, and a technical integration guide. we'll provide a template.
09:27 Elena: do you have marketing assets or co-branded collateral?
09:30 Maya: yes, partner marketing kit and logo usage guidelines.
09:34 Tom: amazing. Any other questions?
09:36 Rajiv: not from me. quick note — we need EU-only deployments to satisfy some customers; can Redwood pin region-only deployments?
09:44 Liam: yes, we can pin model deployments to regions and restrict control plane endpoints to EU. we'll detail in the security doc.
09:52 Maya: ok let's summarize next steps — I'll share the playbook + pricing sheet; Liam prepares benchmark checklist and sample harness; Elena shares infra/network docs; Rajiv coordinates NDA and GTM priorities; schedule tech deep dive week of Jan 11.
10:12 Tom: sounds good. thanks everyone, appreciate the time.
10:16 Maya: thanks all, happy holidays — we'll follow up with links and the partner deck.
10:20 (call ends)
